title: A Preregistered Audit of Dataset Contamination Controls in LLM-for-NetOps Benchmarks
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory audit (study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1) to test whether conservative deterministic contamination detectors (exact normalized token equality; fuzzy 5‑gram shingle overlap; provenance heuristics) flag items in a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample and whether applying preregistered guarded exclusions changes validator‑measured success. Execution used a single hosted LLM (declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini") and a deterministic NetOps verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). The run produced completed_episode_count = 300 episodes (150 item pairs), model_calls_used = 150 (shared_initial_candidate semantics were used), baseline_success_count = 150/150 and guarded_success_count = 150/150. Paired success‑rate difference = 0.0 percentage points (n11 = 150, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0); paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0,0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Crucially, archived artifacts show the confirmatory sample comprised provenance‑stable synthetic tasks and that independent_condition_generation = false produced one shared generation per item; these execution facts materially limited sensitivity for detecting generation‑level contamination in this run. We reconcile preregistration→execution artifacts, report verified execution statistics and validator traces, document the recorded absence of high‑confidence flags, and provide artifact‑grounded recommendations for audit designs that would be sensitive to contamination in web‑sourced benchmarks.

sections.introduction:
Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly being applied to NetOps problems such as intent‑to‑configuration translation and automated configuration repair. Operational adoption requires that benchmarked performance reflect genuine capability rather than artifacts of benchmark contamination (items appearing in model training data) or construct invalidity (templated, low‑complexity tasks). Prior surveys and benchmarks highlight both the promise of LLM‑assisted NetOps and the measurement risks from contamination and weak task constructs [https://openalex.org/W4404602270, https://openalex.org/W4404534210]. To address a methodological aspect of that risk, we preregistered a confirmatory audit testing whether a conservative set of deterministic detectors (exact normalized equality; fuzzy 5‑gram overlap; provenance timestamp heuristics) would (a) flag items at high confidence in a reproducible 150‑item sample and (b) whether applying guarded exclusions (deterministic replacement) would reduce validator‑measured success.

Research question and contribution. The preregistered research question was: under the stated detectors and guarded policy, how prevalent are high‑confidence contamination flags in a reproducible NetOps sample, and how much does applying those controls change the validator pass rate (primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline)? Our contributions are (1) a fully preregistered confirmatory experiment executed end‑to‑end and archived (preregistration SHA‑256 recorded in the execution manifest); (2) exact, artifact‑verified confirmatory statistics for Npairs = 150 with deterministic validator traces; and (3) an explicit preregistration→execution reconciliation that explains why the run produced a degenerate null outcome and prescribes concrete, artifact‑grounded design changes for audits targeting web‑sourced contamination.
sections.related_work:
LLM‑for‑NetOps systems and validation. Recent system and benchmark work demonstrates that LLMs can produce useful configuration artifacts under constrained conditions and that integrating external verifiers or validate–repair loops improves average repair quality [https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.22513, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2606.06212]. Formal network verification tools and localized sub‑specification techniques provide practical oracles for reachability and policy correctness and are commonly recommended as validators in generate–validate pipelines [http://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/viewdoc/summary?doi=10.1.1.300.8659, https://doi.org/10.1007/s11704-026-60308-3].

Evaluation validity and contamination audits. Meta‑analyses emphasize two recurring dangers: contamination (benchmark items—or close paraphrases—appearing in training corpora) and construct invalidity (overly templated tasks). Recent proposals call for artifact‑anchored audits with deterministic detectors, recorded provenance, and predeclared replacement rules [https://openalex.org/W7166900660, https://openalex.org/W4404534210]. Our work implements a conservative subset of these defenses in a preregistered confirmatory design and reports exact artifact‑verified outcomes rather than exploratory, post‑hoc estimates.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimands. The experiment was preregistered as contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1; the preregistration SHA‑256 is recorded in the execution manifest. The primary estimand is the paired success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) over item×model pairs, tested with an exact McNemar two‑sided test and accompanied by a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) per the paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor. Secondary estimands included contamination_rate_per_dataset and templated_vs_realistic subgroup differences; those were prespecified but are only reported here as archive‑supported outputs.

Detectors, thresholds, and guarded policy (archived preregistered rules). The preregistered detectors were (1) exact normalized token equality after canonicalization; (2) fuzzy 5‑gram shingle overlap (Jaccard/overlap) with high‑confidence threshold ≥ 0.80 (and sensitivity thresholds 0.65, 0.50); and (3) provenance timestamp heuristics comparing item timestamps to model cutoff. The guarded policy deterministically excludes only high‑confidence flags (exact match OR fuzzy ≥ 0.80) and replaces them via deterministic retemplating + topology augmentation sampled from the same generator distribution; replacements required embedding similarity (cosine ≥ 0.85) before acceptance. These rules and replacement semantics are archived in the transformation_manifest and preregistration artifacts referenced in the execution bundle.

Sampling, generation semantics, and key execution choices. The preregistration allowed deterministic task generators for reproducibility; the executed sample used deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 to create provenance‑stable synthetic tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") for the confirmatory sample. Critically, execution used independent_condition_generation = false (shared_initial_candidate semantics): when no high‑confidence exclusions occurred, a single shared model generation per item was reused for baseline and guarded episodes. This execution detail is recorded in execution/model_configuration.json (SHA‑256 = a40e96e2...) and task_manifest.jsonl (SHA‑256 = b7c08599...). Because no high‑confidence flags were raised, the shared generation semantics reduced model_calls_used to 150 rather than the maximal 300 planned calls. These documented choices are central to interpreting observed results and are reconciled explicitly in Results.

Verifier and scoring rule. The oracle was deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (version 5.0). For each episode the validator parsed the generated configuration, applied a state‑update model, and evaluated full_intent_constraint_validation: the produced configuration must realize the intended final-state and satisfy workflow constraints. The validator returns a binary pass/fail and a detailed validator_trace (parsed_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, violation codes). Representative validator traces for archived episodes (e.g., task-000001) appear in execution/scoring and are linked by artifact SHA in the bundle.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and deterministic reconciliation. The archive documents: planned_episode_count = 300, completed_episode_count = 300, failed_episode_count = 0, complete_pair_count = 150, and model_calls_used = 150. Deterministic_reconciliation (artifact) confirms consistent episode and provider‑call accounting and reports provider_call_audit: hosted_model_call_event_count = 150, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 150, cache_miss_count = 150, and cross_condition_cache_key_reuse_observed = false. These counts are artifact‑verified (execution manifest and deterministic_reconciliation.json).

Contamination detector outcomes. The preregistered detectors produced zero high‑confidence contamination flags in the executed sample; analysis/contamination_summary.csv contains no flagged rows (artifact SHA‑256 = 389227f0...). The archived detector workflow recorded explicit overlap outputs only for episodes that met flagging criteria or required replacement handling per the preregistration; because no episodes met the high‑confidence threshold, the archive does not contain an aggregated distribution of per‑item fuzzy 5‑gram overlap scores. We therefore report the artifact‑documented absence of high‑confidence flags and the archive’s lack of per‑item overlap summaries rather than inventing overlap statistics that are not present in the bundle.

Validator outcomes and paired analysis. The deterministic_netops_validator_v5 returned pass for all baseline episodes (baseline_success_count = 150/150; baseline_success_rate = 1.0) and for all guarded episodes (guarded_success_count = 150/150; guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table is n11 = 150, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 = c2ba9cdb...). The primary estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline) = 0.0 percentage points; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. These numerical outputs and per‑episode validator traces are archived (analysis/results.json and execution/scoring artifacts).

Representative exemplars. Representative archived episodes illustrate typical artifact structure and validator traces. Example pair-000001/task-000001 shows identical normalized_reference_answer and normalized_response (interface sequence for edge1), parsed_command_count = 4, and validator score = 1 (VALID_CONFIGURATION). The raw responses and validator traces for several exemplars are present under execution/responses and execution/scoring and are referenced by their SHAs in the bundle.
sections.discussion:
Why the run produced a degenerate null. Two execution facts recorded in the archive explain the degenerate paired outcome. First, the confirmatory sample consisted of provenance‑stable synthetic tasks generated by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 (source_identifier: "synthetic-netops:"). Such synthetic provenance reduces the likelihood of high fuzzy‑overlap or exact fingerprint matches to public corpora. Second, independent_condition_generation = false (shared_initial_candidate) was used so that, in the absence of exclusions, a single generation was shared across baseline and guarded episodes. Both facts are preregistered‑allowed choices but together mechanically produced identical baseline and guarded outputs and hence zero discordant pairs. These documented execution choices are the proximate cause of the null paired result and limit inference to the executed sampling regime.

What this execution answers and what it does not. The archived artifacts allow a precise, constrained conclusion: given provenance‑stable synthetic sampling and shared generation semantics, the preregistered detectors raised no high‑confidence flags and guarded exclusions did not alter validator pass rates. The result does not imply absence of contamination in independent web‑sourced benchmarks, does not assess paraphrase‑based leakage, and does not generalize across models. We therefore avoid extrapolating beyond the artifact‑supported scope.

Audit design lessons (artifact‑grounded recommendations). The preregistration→execution reconciliation yields prescriptive, artifact‑grounded recommendations for future contamination audits that seek sensitivity to web‑sourced leakage: (1) sample provenance‑rich public items rather than synthetic provenance items to exercise detectors against real corpora; (2) set independent_condition_generation = true so baseline and guarded conditions are produced by independent generations and cannot collapse into shared outputs; (3) expand to multi‑model sampling and multiple independent seeds to increase the chance of observable discordance; (4) record per‑item fuzzy overlap scores unconditionally (not only when flags occur) so audits can report overlap distributions even when thresholded flags are rare; and (5) complement deterministic overlap detectors with paraphrase‑robust checks and human adjudication for borderline cases. Each recommendation follows directly from archived evidence: execution/model_configuration.json, task_manifest.jsonl, analysis/contamination_summary.csv, and deterministic_reconciliation.json document the current run’s settings and the empty flag set that motivates these changes.

Threats to validity and operational implications. Internal validity: shared generation semantics and single‑model scope reduce sensitivity to generation‑level contamination; these are documented preregistered choices rather than post‑hoc deviations. Construct validity: the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces a specified set of functional constraints (full_intent_constraint_validation) but does not cover every operational impact dimension (e.g., side‑effects outside the modeled state). External validity: a single model (gpt‑5‑mini) and provenance‑stable synthetic tasks limit generalization to web‑sourced benchmarks and other LLM families. Conclusion validity: sample size was preregistered (150 pairs) but power to detect small paired differences is reduced under single‑model shared‑generation semantics; the preregistration’s power guidance and sensitivity curves are archived and should inform future designs.

Reproducibility and artifact verification. All experiment artifacts, validator traces, sampling seeds, and analysis inputs/outputs are archived in the execution bundle. Key artifact SHAs recorded in the Disclosure Statement (for example, execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = a40e96e2..., execution/task_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 = b7c08599..., analysis input/results SHA‑256 = 5337998d...) permit independent verification that (a) the confirmatory sample used synthetic provenance tasks, (b) independent_condition_generation = false, (c) model_calls_used = 150, and (d) the paired contingency table is n11 = 150 with no flagged episodes in analysis/contamination_summary.csv. Because the archive did not record unconditional per‑item fuzzy overlap distributions for this run, auditors seeking overlap summaries must request unconditional logging in future executions or perform detector re‑runs on archived raw responses.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired audit of conservative contamination detectors for LLM‑for‑NetOps evaluation. For the executed, provenance‑stable synthetic sample with shared generation semantics, we observed zero preregistered high‑confidence contamination flags and identical validator pass rates (150/150 baseline and guarded). The degenerate null is artifact‑supported and stems from the documented sampling and generation choices; it does not imply that public, web‑sourced benchmarks are contamination‑free nor that the preregistered detectors would fail under richer sampling. We provide a transparent preregistration→execution reconciliation, present exact artifact‑verified statistics and validator traces, and offer concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations—provenance‑rich sampling, independent generation per condition, multi‑model scope, unconditional detector logging, and paraphrase‑sensitive checks—to increase audit sensitivity in future studies. All experiment artifacts and verification SHAs are archived per the execution bundle and listed succinctly in the Disclosure Statement below.

limitations: Single‑model execution (gpt‑5-mini) — results do not generalize across other LLM families, sizes, or training corpora.

Sampled items were provenance‑stable synthetic/deterministically generated tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") for this run; absence of high‑confidence flags here may not reflect contamination prevalence in real‑world, web‑crawled benchmarks.

Generation semantics used shared_initial_candidate across baseline and guarded conditions (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical model outputs when no exclusions occurred and thus limiting sensitivity to interventions that rely on independent re‑generation.

Contamination detection relied on preregistered conservative heuristics (exact match and fuzzy 5‑gram overlap thresholds); subtler contamination patterns (paraphrased memorization, partial leakage) may escape these heuristics and require richer provenance or manual adjudication.

Passing the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 indicates satisfaction of the checked functional constraints but does not imply comprehensive production readiness or absence of semantic regressions outside the validator's scope.
